Transaction price allocated to the remaining performance obligations
	
Performance obligations related to sale of energy: 
	
Revenue from sale of energy is accounted for based on tariff rates approved by the CERC (except items indicated as provisional) 
as modified by the orders of Appellate Tribunal for Electricity to the extent applicable. In case of power stations, where the tariff 
rates are yet to be approved/items indicated provisional by the CERC in their orders, provisional rates are adopted considering 
the applicable CERC Tariff Regulations. Revenue from sale of energy is recognized once the electricity has been delivered to the 
beneficiary and is measured through a regular review of usage meters. Beneficiaries are billed on a periodic and regular basis. 
Therefore, transaction price to be allocated to remaining performance obligations cannot be determined reliably for the entire 
duration of the contract.
	
Performance obligations related to other contracts:	
	
	
	
	
	
	
For rest of the contracts, transaction price for remaining performance obligations amounts to ₹ 462.68 crore (31 March 2025: 
₹ 477.99 crore) which shall be received over the contract period in proportion of the work performed/services provided by the 
Group.

e. 	
The Environment (Protection) Rules, 2015, as amended from time to time, issued by the Ministry of Environment, Forest 
and Climate Change (MoEF&CC), introduced emission norms on NOx for thermal power plants and prescribed timelines for 
achieving compliance. The amended rules further stipulate that non-retiring thermal power plants, remaining non-compliant 
for NOx emissions, beyond the prescribed timelines are liable to pay Environmental Compensation based on the quantum of 
electricity generated and the duration of non-compliance. However, the matter is sub-judice before Hon’ble Supreme Court 
of India.
	
Further, MoEF&CC has prescribed a phased compliance framework for achieving 100% utilisation of fly ash generated from 
thermal power plants. The compliance of the same with the prescribed utilisation targets and related statutory implications, 
if any, would be determined upon completion of relevant compliance cycle for each thermal power station.
B. 	 Contingent assets	
	
	
	
	
(i) 	
While determining the tariff for some of the Parent Company’s power stations, CERC has disallowed certain capital 
expenditure incurred by the Parent Company. The Parent Company aggrieved over such issues has filed appeals with the 
Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL)/Hon’ble Supreme Court against the tariff orders issued by the CERC. Based on past 
experience, the Parent Company believes that a favourable outcome is probable. However, it is impracticable to estimate the 
financial effect of the same as its receipt is dependent on the outcome of the judgement.	
	
	
	
(ii)	
 Coal companies have disputed some of the grade slippages confirmed by CIMFR(third party sampler)  in favour of the 
Company and have approached referee challenging the CIMFR results. The referee results are binding on both the parties. 
Considering the uncertainty involved in the outcome of referee results, the Company has not recognised claims arising out 
of favourable CIMFR results pending receipt of referee results challenged by the coal companies, considering the provisions 
of Ind AS 37.  It is impracticable to estimate the financial effect of the same as its receipt is dependent on the outcome of 
the referee results which is wholly not within the control of the Company. Not withstanding the above, the outcome of the 
referee results shall be dealt with as per the provisions of CERC Tariff Regulations.  	
	
	
	
	
(iii)	 CERC (Terms & Conditions of Tariff) Regulations 2019-24 provide for levy of Late Payment Surcharge by generating 
company in case of delay in payment by beneficiaries beyond 45 days from the date of presentation of bill. However, in 
view of significant uncertainties in the ultimate collection from some of the beneficiaries against partial bills as resolved 
by the management, an amount of ₹ 604.32 crore as at 31 March 2026 (31 March 2025: ₹ 1,074.31 crore) has not been 
recognised.

INDEPENDENT AUDITORS’ REPORT
To
The Members of NTPC Limited
Report on the Audit of the Consolidated Financial Statements
Opinion
We have audited the accompanying Consolidated Financial Statements of NTPC Limited (hereinafter referred to as “the Holding Company”) 
and its subsidiaries (the Holding Company and its subsidiaries together referred to as “the Group”), and its share of profit/ loss in joint 
ventures, which comprise the Consolidated Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2026, the Consolidated Statement of Profit and Loss (including 
Other Comprehensive Income), the Consolidated Statement of Changes in Equity and the Consolidated Statement of Cash Flows for the 
year then ended, and notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements, including a summary of the Material accounting policies and other 
explanatory information for the year ended on that date (hereinafter referred to as “Consolidated Financial Statements”).
In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us and based on the consideration of reports 
of other auditors on separate Financial Statements and on the other financial information of the subsidiaries and joint ventures referred to 
in the Other Matters section below, the aforesaid Consolidated Financial Statements give the information required by the Companies Act, 
2013 (‘the Act’) in the manner so required and give a true and fair view in conformity with the Indian Accounting Standards prescribed under 
section 133 of the Act, read with the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015, as amended (“Ind AS”) and other accounting 
principles generally accepted in India, of the consolidated state of affairs (financial position) of the  Group and its joint ventures as at 31 
March 2026, and their consolidated net profit (financial performance including other comprehensive income), their consolidated changes in 
equity and consolidated cash flows for the year ended on that date.
Basis for Opinion
We conducted our audit of the Consolidated Financial Statements in accordance with the Standards on Auditing (SAs) specified under 
section 143(10) of the Act. Our responsibilities under those Standards are further described in the Auditor’s Responsibilities for the Audit of 
the Consolidated Financial Statements section of our report. We are independent of the Group and its Joint Ventures in accordance with 
the ‘Code of Ethics’ issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) together with the ethical requirements that are relevant 
to our audit of the Consolidated Financial Statements under the provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder, and we have fulfilled 
our other ethical responsibilities in accordance with these requirements and the ICAI’s Code of Ethics. We believe that the audit evidence 
obtained by us and the audit evidence obtained by the other auditors in terms of their reports referred in the Other Matters section below, is 
sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our audit opinion on the Consolidated Financial Statements.
Emphasis of Matter
We draw attention relating to accounting of revenue and expenses which were transferred to fly ash utilization reserve fund during the 
financial year 2024-25 that has now been accounted for in line with the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions 
of Tariff) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2026. Further, taking guidance from the principles of this amendment, the Group has also 
accounted for the accumulated amount in the ash utilization reserve fund as at 1 April 2024 amounting to ₹ 919.09 crore, as non-tariff 
income (NTI) to be shared with the beneficiaries. (Refer Note No. 25 (f))
Our opinion is not modified in respect of the aforesaid matter.
Key Audit Matters
Key audit matters are those matters that, in our professional judgment, were of most significance in our audit of the Consolidated Financial 
Statements of the current period. These matters were addressed in the context of our audit of the Consolidated Financial Statements as a 
whole, and in forming our opinion thereon, and we do not provide a separate opinion on these matters. For each matter below, description 
of how our audit addressed the matter is provided in that context. Considering the requirement of Standard on Auditing (SA 600) on ‘Using 
the work of Another Auditor’ including materiality, below Key Audit Matters have been reproduced from the Independent Auditors’ report on 
the audit of Standalone Financial Statements of the Holding Company. 
S. No.
Key Audit Matters
How our audit addressed the Key Audit Matters
1.
Recognition and Measurement of revenue from Sale of 
Energy
The Holding Company records revenue from sale of energy as 
per the principles enunciated under Ind AS 115, based on tariff 
approved by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission 
(CERC) as modified by the orders of Appellate Authorities. 
Pending issue of provisional/final tariff order w.e.f. 01 April, 
2024 capacity charges has been provisionally recognised 
considering the applicable CERC Tariff Regulations 2024.
This is considered as key audit matter due to the nature and 
extent of estimates made as per the CERC Tariff Regulations, 
which leads to recognition and measurement of revenue from 
sale of energy being complex and judgmental.
(Refer Note No. 42 to the Consolidated Financial Statements, 
read with the Material Accounting Policy No. C.12)
We have obtained an understanding of the CERC Tariff 
Regulations, orders, circulars, guidelines and the Company’s 
internal circulars and procedures in respect of recognition and 
measurement of revenue from sale of energy comprising of 
capacity and energy charges and adopted the following audit 
procedures:
-	
Evaluated and tested the effectiveness of the Company’s 
design of internal controls relating to recognition and 
measurement of revenue from sale of energy.
-	
Examined the Holding Company’s material accounting 
policies with respect to assessing compliance with Ind AS 
115 “Revenue from Contract with Customers”.
-	
Verified the accounting of revenue from sale of energy 
based on provisional/ final tariff computed as per the 
principles of CERC Tariff Regulations 2024.
-	
Assessed the disclosures in accordance with the 
requirements of Ind AS 115 “Revenue from Contract with 
Customers”.
Based on the above procedure performed, the recognition, 
measurement and disclosures of revenue from sale of energy 
are considered to be adequate and reasonable.
2.
Impairment assessment of Property, Plant and Equipment 
(PPE)
The Holding Company has a material operational asset base 
(PPE) relating to generation of electricity and is one of the 
components for determining the tariff as per the CERC Tariff 
Regulations, which may be vulnerable to impairment. 
We considered this as a key audit matter as the carrying value 
of PPE requires impairment assessment based on the future 
expected cash flows associated with the power plants (Cash 
generating units). 
(Refer Note No. 63 to the Consolidated Financial Statements, 
read with the Material Accounting Policy No. C.16)
We have obtained an understanding and tested the design 
and operating effectiveness of controls as established by the 
Company’s management for impairment assessment of PPE.
We evaluated the Holding Company’s process of impairment 
assessment in assessing the appropriateness of the impairment 
model including the independent assessment of discount rate, 
economic growth rate, terminal value etc.
We evaluated and checked the calculations of the cash flow 
forecasts prepared by the Holding Company taking into 
consideration the CERC (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) 
Regulations, 2024 (applicable for the tariff period of 5 years from 
1 April 2024 to 31 March 2029) along with the aforementioned 
assumptions. 
Based on the above procedures performed, we observed that 
the Company’s impairment assessment of the PPE is adequate 
and reasonable.
3.
Deferred Tax Asset relating to MAT Credit Entitlement
The holding company has recognised deferred tax asset 
relating to MAT credit entitlement. Utilisation of MAT credit will 
result in lower outflow of Income Tax in future years.
The recoverability of this deferred tax asset relating to MAT 
credit entitlement is dependent upon the generation of sufficient 
future taxable profits to utilise such entitlement within the 
stipulated period prescribed under the Income Tax Act, 2025.
We have obtained an understanding for recognition of deferred 
tax asset relating to MAT credit entitlement including the 
management’s judgement.
We further assessed the related forecasts of future taxable 
profits and evaluated the reasonableness of the considerations

Report on the Internal Financial Controls with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements under Clause (i) of Sub-section 3 of 
Section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013 (“the Act”)
In conjunction with our audit of the Consolidated Financial Statements of the Company as of and for the year ended 31 March 2026, we have 
audited the internal financial controls with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements of NTPC Limited (hereinafter referred to as “the 
Holding Company”) and its subsidiaries (the Holding Company and its subsidiaries together referred to as “the Group”), and joint ventures, 
which are companies incorporated in India, as of that date.
Management’s Responsibility for Internal Financial Controls
The respective Board of Directors of the Holding Company, its subsidiaries, and joint ventures, which are companies incorporated in India, 
are responsible for establishing and maintaining internal financial controls based on the internal controls over financial reporting criteria 
established by the respective companies considering the essential components of internal control stated in the Guidance Note on Audit of 
Internal Financial Controls over Financial Reporting issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI). These responsibilities 
include the design, implementation and maintenance of adequate internal financial controls that were operating effectively for ensuring 
the orderly and efficient conduct of its business, including adherence to the respective company’s policies, the safeguarding of its assets, 
the prevention and detection of frauds and errors, the accuracy and completeness of the accounting records, and the timely preparation of 
reliable financial information, as required under the Act.
Auditors’ Responsibility
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Company’s internal financial controls with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements 
based on our audit. We conducted our audit in accordance with the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls over Financial 
Reporting (the “Guidance Note”) and the Standards on Auditing prescribed under section 143(10) of the Act, to the extent applicable to an 
audit of internal financial controls with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements. Those Standards and the Guidance Note require 
that we comply with ethical requirements and plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether adequate internal 
financial controls with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements was established and maintained and if such controls operated 
effectively in all material respects.
Our audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the adequacy of the internal financial control with reference to 
Consolidated Financial Statements and their operating effectiveness. Our audit of internal financial controls with reference to Consolidated 
Financial Statements included obtaining an understanding of internal financial controls with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements, 
assessing the risk that a material weakness exists, and testing and evaluating the design and operating effectiveness of internal control 
based on the assessed risk. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgement, including the assessment of the risks of material 
misstatement of the Consolidated Financial Statements, whether due to fraud or error.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained and the audit evidence obtained by the other auditors of the subsidiaries and joint 
ventures, incorporated in India, in terms of their reports referred to in the ‘Other Matters’ paragraph below, is sufficient and appropriate to 
provide a basis for our audit opinion on the internal financial controls of the Group and its Joint Venture Companies incorporated in India, 
with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements.
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements
A company’s internal financial control with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements is a process designed to provide reasonable 
assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of Consolidated Financial Statements for external purposes in 
accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s internal financial control with reference to Consolidated Financial 
Statements includes those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately

in the Company.
Item No. 8: Raising of funds up to ₹12,000 Crore through issue of 
Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs/Bonds) on Private 
Placement basis
The Company is the largest power producer in India. As the 
Company is under capacity expansion mode, a major portion of the 
capital expenditure requirement of the Company has to be funded 
by debt. The Company borrows in the form of Non-Convertible 
Debentures (NCDs)/ Bonds, rupee term loans from banks and 
financial institutions, foreign currency borrowings, foreign currency 
bonds etc. The NCDs/ Bond are raised by the Company under a 
public issue route or through private placement basis.
In addition to the capital expenditure requirement as explained 
above, the Company also needs to borrow for meeting its working 
capital requirement and other general corporate purposes, which is 
partly proposed to be met through the issuance of NCDs/Bonds.
The provisions of Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013, read 
with Rule 14(1) of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of 
Securities) Rules, 2014, require the Company to seek a Special 
Resolution from its shareholders for raising the NCDs on a private 
placement basis. However, in case of offer or invitation for “non-
convertible debentures”, it shall be sufficient if the Company passes 
a prior Special Resolution once a year for all the offers or invitations 
for such debentures during the year.
In view of the above, approval of the shareholders of the Company 
is being sought to authorise the Board of Directors to make 
offer(s) or invitation(s) to subscribe to the secured/unsecured, 
redeemable, taxable/tax-free, cumulative/non-cumulative, non-
convertible debentures (“NCDs/Bonds”) up to ₹12,000 Crore in one 
or more tranches/series not exceeding 12 (twelve), through private 
placement, in domestic market for capex, working capital and 
general corporate purposes during the period commencing from 
the date of passing of Special Resolution till completion of one year 
thereof or the date of next Annual General Meeting in the financial 
year 2027-28, whichever is earlier, subject to ceiling approved by the 
shareholders under Section 180 (1) (c) of Companies Act, 2013.
The Board of Directors of the Company in its Meeting held on
24th July 2026 has approved the proposal and recommends the 
passing of the proposed Special Resolution.
The Directors or key managerial personnel or their relatives do not 
have any concern or interest, financial or otherwise, in passing of the 
said Special Resolution, except to the extent of their shareholding in 
the Company.

Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi laid the Foundation Stone for ASHVINI’s 
Mahi Banswara Rajasthan Atomic Power Project - MBRAPP (4X700 MW) at Banswara 
on the 25 September 2025. Located in Banswara district of Rajasthan, the project 
entails an investment of around Rs 42,000 crore. Upon completion, this project will 
be one of the largest nuclear plants in the country supplying reliable base load energy 
and will strengthen India’s position in the environmental stewardship & evolving 
nuclear energy landscape.
MBRAPP is being developed by Anushakti Vidhyut Nigam Ltd (ASHVINI)— with joint 
participation of NPCIL (51%) and NTPC (49%) pooling the financial, technological,

and project expertise of both companies.
MBRAPP will comprise of four indigenous 700 MW Pressurized Heavy Water Reactors 
(PHWRs) with advanced safety features - also known as IPHWR 700 - designed and 
developed by NPCIL. The project is part of India’s broader “fleet mode” initiative, 
where ten identical 700 MW reactors are being built across India under uniform design 
and procurement plans. Three such reactors have been commissioned, and Mahi 
Banswara is also part of the fleet. This approach promotes the spirit of Atmanirbhar 
Bharat and brings in cost efficiencies, faster deployment, and consolidated operational 
expertise.
MBRAPP will supply clean, affordable and reliable power to Rajasthan and other 
beneficiaries. This will create direct & indirect employment opportunities and will 
support local communities, businesses, and industries, supporting the economic 
growth and prosperity in the state and the country.

Energising India’s Growth, 
Powering the Transition
Aligning NTPC’s growth with India’s vision of Viksit Bharat @2047 and Net Zero @2070
India has set itself two defining goals for the decades ahead: to become a developed nation Viksit Bharat by 2047, the centenary of its 
independence, and to achieve Net Zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2070. For NTPC, India’s largest integrated power utility, supporting 
both goals lies at the heart of our purpose and our long-term strategy.
The world's energy system is undergoing a rapid transformation 
as governments and businesses accelerate their decarbonisation 
efforts. According to Net Zero Tracker, 137 countries have 
already established net-zero targets, while 145 countries have 
announced or are considering net-zero commitments. Reflecting 
this global shift, the International Energy Agency (IEA) reports 
that clean energy is attracting an increasingly larger share of 
new investment in power generation worldwide.Solar, wind 
and battery storage are being added to record levels

each year, 
supported by a sustained fall in technology costs over the past 
decade. At the same time, governments are placing renewed 
emphasis on energy security, resilient supply chains for critical 
minerals, and the need to keep energy affordable through a 
period of global uncertainty.
India approaches this transition as one of the world’s fastest-
growing major economies and its most populous nation, even as 
its per-capita energy use and emissions remain well below the 
global average. India’s transition is therefore distinctive: it must 
serve a large and rising demand for energy while steadily reducing 
the carbon intensity of that energy. This approach is guided by the 
principles of equity and common but differentiated responsibilities, 
as reflected in India’s commitments under the UNFCCC and its 
Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy.
The Global Energy Transition
NITI Aayog’s study, Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero, 
provides a comprehensive assessment of how India can pursue 
rapid development and deep decarbonization together. As per its 
scenarios, India’s economy is projected to grow from around USD 
4.2 trillion in 2025 to about USD 30 trillion by 2047, accompanied by 
rapid urbanization and a multi-fold increase in the output of steel, 
cement and other materials as the country moves closer to global 
per-capita consumption levels.
A notable feature of these scenarios is that energy demand 
grows far more slowly than the economy. Final energy demand is 
projected to rise only about 2.1 to 2.6 times by 2070, even as GDP 
expands roughly elevenfold, on account of greater electrification, 
improved energy efficiency and circularity. Electricity is at the centre 
of this shift. Its share of final energy consumption is projected to 
rise from around 21% at present to as much as 60% by 2070, while 
total electricity demand could grow six to eight times over the 
same period, lifting per-capita consumption towards the levels of 
advan

ced economies. The pace at which the power grid becomes 
cleaner will, in large measure, determine the pace of decarbonization 
across the wider economy.
Meeting India’s electricity needs cleanly calls for a transformation 
of unprecedented scale. NITI Aayog’s Net Zero Scenario indicates 
that total installed generation capacity could grow roughly fourteen 
times by 2070, with renewable energy forming the new core of 
the grid. Solar becomes the backbone, with capacity potentially 
exceeding 5,000 GW, complemented by more than 1,000 GW of 
wind, including offshore wind off the coasts of Gujarat and Tamil 
Nadu. The share of non-fossil capacity rises from around 40% at 
present to close to 98% by 2070.
India’s Twin Goals: Viksit Bharat and Net Zero
Transforming the Power Sector
As variable renewables come to dominate, energy storage and 
firm power become essential to maintaining reliability. In the 
same scenarios, battery energy storage is projected to scale from 
negligible levels today to 2,500–3,000 GW by 2070, supported 
by 150–165 GW of pumped hydro. Nuclear power emerges as 
a strategic pillar of firm, low-carbon generation, scaling from 
around 8 GW today (Central Electricity Authority) towards 100 GW 
by 2047, in line with the national nuclear mission, and potentially 
300 GW by 2070 in NITI Aayog’s projections, with small modular 
reactors playing an increasing role.
Coal continues to play a vital role through the transition. In the near-
to-medium term, the existing coal fleet remains important for grid 
reliability and for meeting demand during periods of high system 
stress. In these scenarios, coal capacity is expected to peak 
around the mid-2040s before declining as long-duration storage 
and clean alternatives mature. The emphasis, therefore, is on 
improving the efficiency, flexibility and environmental performance 
of the coal fleet so that it can support a renewable-rich grid, while 
avoiding long-term lock-ins. This balanced approach, which 
sec

ures reliability even as the system decarbonises, is precisely 
where a utility of NTPC’s scale and operating experience adds the 
greatest value.

For sectors that are difficult to electrify directly, such as heavy 
industry and long-distance transport, green hydrogen emerges 
as a key clean-energy carrier. It can serve as a reducing agent in 
green steelmaking, a feedstock for green ammonia and fertilisers, 
a cleaner input for refineries, and the basis for green methanol 
and ammonia in shipping. Under the National Green Hydrogen 
Mission, India aims to produce 5 million tonnes of green hydrogen 
each year by 2030, while NITI Aayog’s Net Zero Scenario projects 
demand rising towards 25 million tonnes by 2050 and around 50 
million tonnes by 2070. Because most green hydrogen is produced 
through renewable-powered electrolysis, its growth is closely linked 
to the expansion of clean power.
The transition is capital-intensive. NITI Aayog estimates cumulative 
investment of around USD 22.7 trillion by 2070 under the Net Zero 
Scenario, with the power sector accounting for over half of the total, 
reflecting its central role in electrifying the wider economy. This 
implies average annual flows of close to USD 500 billion, against 
actual energy investment of about USD 135 billion in 2024 (IEA). 
Mobilising capital on this scale, attracting low-cost finance, and 
building domestic manufacturing and innovation capacity are 
among the defining tasks of the coming decades.
The human dimension of the transition is equally important. NITI 
Aayog’s assessment of the social implications of the transition 
notes that more than 150 districts depend significantly on fossil-
fuel supply chains, and that coal-based power and mining together 
sustain millions of formal and informal livelihoods. Encouragin

gly, 
the same analysis finds that the Net Zero pathway is expected 
to create more energy-sector jobs than it displaces, with around 
one million additional energy jobs by 2050, alongside substantial 
gains in construction and clean-technology manufacturing, 
provided the transition is managed with care through reskilling, 
livelihood diversification and support for affected communities. 
NTPC remains committed to a just energy transition, ensuring that 
progress towards a cleaner energy system continues to create 
opportunity and shared prosperity.
As the nation’s largest power producer, NTPC has a central role 
to play in this transformation. With an installed and commercial 
group capacity of over 90 GW, NTPC meets close to one-fourth of 
India’s electricity requirement. The Company has built its standing 
on reliability, operational excellence and affordable power, and is 
now applying the same discipline to one of the most ambitious 
diversification journeys in the global power sector. In line with our 
vision to be the world’s leading power company, accelerating India’s 
growth along with energy transition, the company is strengthening 
its existing core business while building a new core in renewables, 
storage, nuclear, green hydrogen and green chemicals.
At the centre of this strategy is The Brighter Plan, NTPC’s roadmap 
to reshape its portfolio around clean energy to address the triple 
bottom line. The Company has set a target of 60 GW of renewable 
energy capacity by 2032, as part of a planned total capacity of 
around 149 GW, with non-fossil sources expected to constitute 
nearly half of the portfolio. This is envisaged to scale up to 244 GW 
by 2037, out of which 136 GW will come from RE portfolio, and the 
non-fossil fuel based capacity will gain 60% of the capacity share. 
To drive this growth, NTPC has carved out and listed NTPC Green 
Energy Limited (NGEL), its dedicated renewable energy arm, which 
has crossed 10 GW of installed capacity and is

developing gigawatt-
scale solar, wind and hybrid parks, including the flagship Khavda 
complex in Gujarat, under the Ultra Mega Renewable Energy Power 
Park model. To champion the other part of the clean energy portfolio 
by addition of Nuclear Energy, the company is already in process 
to setup its first nuclear power project in Banswara, Rajasthan 
under its joint venture with Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd 
(NPCIL), while setting up another wholly owned subsidiary NTPC 
Parmanu Urja Nigam Limited (NPUNL) to add nuclear capacities 
across India.

gy transition. Because electricity will increasingly

As the country’s largest generator, NTPC is closely involved in this

Our strategy is aligned with the levers the nation must deploy renewable 
energy at gigawatt pace, building the storage and firm capacity that 
make a renewables-rich grid reliable, advancing nuclear power and

growth with the national interest — strengthening energy security 
through greater reliance on indigenous resources, reducing exposure 
to imported fuels, and creating new green industries and jobs.
The journey to 2047 and 2070 will require significant capital, 
sustained innovation, strong partnerships and steady resolve. 
NTPC is committed to this journey: to deliver reliable and affordable 
power today, while investing decisively in the clean energy system 
of tomorrow. In doing so, the Company reaffirms its commitment to 
energizing India’s growth and to building a cleaner, greener and more 
prosperous future for the nation.

Letter to the Shareholders 
Dear Shareholders,
The global energy landscape is changing rapidly. Geopolitical 
tensions, supply chain disruptions, commodity price volatility, 
climate commitments, and the expansion of digital infrastructure 
have made energy security a strategic priority for nations across 
the world. Energy security has never received this level of attention 
in history. Recent events have shown that economic growth, 
industrial competitiveness, and national resili

ence are closely 
linked to the availability of reliable and affordable energy.
For India, this has reinforced the need for a diversified and resilient 
energy ecosystem. The country’s installed power capacity has 
crossed 550 GW, with non-fossil sources accounting for more 
than 52% of the total. India has also achieved the milestone of 50% 
non-fossil installed capacity five years ahead of target, creating a 
strong foundation for sustainable growth.
India’s economic momentum remains robust, with GDP growth 
estimated at around 7.7%. Simultaneously, the country’s power 
demand is projected to grow by 6–6.5% annually over the coming 
years. Peak demand crossed 270 GW in FY26 and is projected by 
CEA to reach about 459 GW by FY36. Expansion in manufacturing, 
infrastructure, electric mobility, urbanisation, and digital services 
is expected to sustain this growth. In addition, the rapid expansion 
of AI, cloud computing, and data centres will increase the demand 
for reliable, high-quality, round-the-clock power.
In this environment, NTPC is well positioned to support India’s 
growth. Our installed capacity reached 89.1 GW in FY26, more 
than doubling over the last decade. During FY26, we achieved 
our highest-ever annual capacity addition of 9.62 GW, with nearly 
60% of the additions coming from renewable energy sources. 
NTPC generated 432.2 billion units of electricity during the year, 
contributing 23.6% of India’s total power generation and reinforcing 
our role as a key pillar of the country’s energy system.
Our coal-based stations delivered a plant load factor of 72.04%, 
significantly above the national average, reflecting the efficiency 
and reliability of our operations. Our trading arm NTPC Vidyut 
Vyapar Nigam Limited traded 46.38 billion units of power during 
the year.
Strengthening domestic energy capabilities remains a key priority. 
NTPC Mining Limited has emerged as the third-largest coal 
mining company in India, with six operational mines and thr

ee 
under development. Captive coal production reached 48.65 million 
tonnes in FY26, which is nearly 18% of our annual requirement, 
helping improve fuel security and operational self-reliance.
We are also investing in the future of the utility sector. Artificial 
intelligence, predictive analytics, and advanced forecasting tools 
are being integrated across our generation, renewable, mining, and 
maintenance operations. These technologies will improve plant 
availability, optimise operations, reduce costs, and strengthen 
safety.
At the same time, we are expanding our capabilities in pumped 
storage projects and battery energy storage systems to support 
renewable integration and grid stability. We are also investing 
in next-generation energy storage technologies, including CO₂-
based energy storage systems and vanadium redox flow batteries, 
to strengthen grid flexibility and long-duration storage capabilities. 
These technologies have the potential to complement conventional 
battery systems by providing longer discharge durations, improved 
operational flexibility. Our investments in these emerging storage 
solutions are aimed at building capabilities that will support future 
grid requirements and contribute to the development of a more 
resilient and reliable power system.
We have also entered the nuclear sector with the Mahi Banswara 
project in Rajasthan. In addition, studies are being undertaken 
across 34 sites in 13 States for future nuclear project development 
opportunities, and a site selection report for one location has been 
submitted to the Department of Atomic Energy for consideration.
Our thermal fleet will continue to play an important role in India’s 
energy mix. Through investments in emission control systems, 
flexible operations, biomass co-firing, water conservation, ash 
utilisation, and carbon management initiatives, we are making our 
thermal assets more efficient and environmentally responsible.
FY26 was also a strong year financially

. We achieved our highest-
ever consolidated Profit After Tax of ₹27,546 crore, up 15% over 
the previous year, while standalone Profit After Tax increased 
18% to ₹23,162 crore. Consolidated earnings per share stood at 
₹27.90. We have maintained our record of consistent dividend 
payments for over three decades, with a dividend payout ratio of 
around 37.68% for FY26.
Looking ahead, NTPC’s growth will be guided by four priorities: 
meeting India’s rising electricity demand, strengthening energy 
security through domestic capabilities, expanding clean and 
flexible energy infrastructure, and leveraging digital technologies

NTPC continues to strengthen its position as India's largest 
integrated power utility by expanding and modernising its 
conventional generation portfolio. Thermal power remains the 
backbone of the country's energy system, providing reliable 
baseload electricity to support economic growth and facilitate 
large-scale renewable energy integration. The Company is 
enhancing operational efficiency through adoption of advanced 
technologies, digitalisation, flexible plant operations and life 
extension initiatives, while simultaneously reducing emissions

through improved efficiency, biomass co-firing, flue gas 
desulphurisation systems and water conservation measures.

play a critical role in maintaining grid reliability while supporting

Biomass co-firing is an integral component of NTPC's strategy to 
decarbonise conventional power generation while strengthening 
domestic fuel security. As the first utility in India to commercialise 
biomass co-firing at scale, NTPC has demonstrated the use 
of agro-residue-based biomass pellets as a partial substitute 
for coal, enabling the production of renewable energy through 
existing thermal power infrastructure. The initiative contributes to 
reducing greenhouse gas emissions, mitigating stubble burning, 
promoting sustainable agricultural residue management, and 
generating additional income opportunities for farmers and rural 
entrepreneurs. During FY 2025-26, the NTPC Group sourced 1.52 
million tonnes of biomass, more than doubling the previous year's 
procurement, and expanded commercial biomass co-firing across 
multiple thermal power stations. The Company has awarded 
contracts for the supply of over 3 million tonnes of biomass 
pellets covering 22 stations, while also increasing the utilisation of 
municipal solid waste-derived torrefied charcoal as an alternative 
green fuel. These initiatives reinforce NTPC's commitment to 
cleaner thermal generation, circular economy principles and 
sustainable rural development.

Risk Management and Governance 
At NTPC, we view risk management as a strategic driver, integral 
to achieving our business objectives responsibly and sustainably. 
Given the diverse business models and operations across NTPC 
Limited and its JVs/Subsidiaries, it is essential for each entity 
to manage risks effectively. This entails establishing robust 
risk governance frameworks and structures, as well as the 
meticulous, timely identification, classification, and assessment 
of risks. Prioritizing risks based on their potential impact on the 
business and likelihood of occurrence is crucial, followed by the 
implementation of mitigation strategies. 
Additionally, fostering a strong risk culture, coupled with 
monitoring and reporting mechanisms, further enhances risk 
management practices. Moreover, our approach extends beyond 
conventional business risks to encompass environmental, social, 
and governance (ESG) related risks. This holistic perspective 
acknowledges the interconnectedness of risks across the entire 
organization, its stakeholders, and the value chain. 
Risk Governance
Risk management is integrated into our system of governance to 
provide effective oversight and support the consideration of risks 
when making key decisions or setting strategic goals. The Risk 
Management policy guides the company’s approach to managing 
risks. It covers the identification of internal and external risks 
specific to the organization, which includes operational, legal & 
compliance, strategic, technological, financial and environmental 
& social risks.
The internal audit team acts as a third line of defence and 
independently assure company's risk management practices. 
Notably, NTPC is among the first CPSEs to have its Enterprise 
Risk Management (ER

M) policy audited by statutory auditors, 
underscoring its commitment to robust risk governance. 
Established in 2015, the Board-level Risk Management Committee 
(RMC) oversees Enterprise Risk Management for the Company, 
Chaired by the Director (Projects) and comprising of key directors 
and the Chief Risk Officer. The Committee ensures comprehensive 
coverage of the holistic risk environment across categories such 
as strategic, operational, financial, compliance, and emerging 
risks. The RMC actively facilitates the identification, assessment, 
prioritization, and mitigation of risks within these groups 
through timely action plans. This structured approach enhances 
organizational resilience, drives informed decision-making, and 
contributes to long-term value creation for stakeholders.
The Chief Risk Officer (CRO) at NTPC holds a critical role in 
overseeing the Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) process 
and reporting its compliance to the Board of Directors. The key 
responsibilities include designing, reviewing, and continuously 
enhancing ERM processes; preparing comprehensive enterprise-
wide risk reports for the Risk Management Committee and the 
Board; and regularly updating them on the ERM status and key 
risks with actionable insights. The CRO also ensures effective 
implementation and validation of the ERM Policy across all 
functions, assists in developing and refining ERM policies to 
strengthen the company’s resilience, and promotes a strong 
ERM culture through awareness and capacity-building initiatives 
throughout the organization.
The Company’s risk management framework is aligned with the 
principles of ISO 31000, enabling a systematic and consistent 
approach to risk identification, assessment, mitigation, monitoring, 
and reporting, and supporting informed decision-making and 
long-term value creation.

the power sector. These risks include policy shifts in

Business Continuity Plan (BCP)

established comprehensive Business Continuity Plans (BCP). As

lated services. In such circumstances,

resources accordingly. BCPs are developed for business units 
in alignment with the National Disaster Management Authority 
guidelines, NTPC’s Emergency Response Planning guidance, and 
the Company’s Cyber Security Policy.

drills, internal audits, and continuous learning. This enables us 
to improve preparedness and respond effectively to operational 
disruptions.

Management of Financial Capital
NTPC’s capital allocation is guided by a structured decision 
framework prioritizing system reliability, sustainability, and long-
term value creation. Investment decisions are evaluated through 
financial and non-financial lenses, including expected returns 
across the asset life, project risks, execution readiness, regulatory 
alignment, and contribution to transition objectives. We prioritize 
projects that strengthen reliability, flexibility, and efficiency while 
enabling a higher share of renewables in the grid.
In a regulated and largely contract-backed power sector, cash 
realization and receivables management are central to financial 
resilience. NTPC sustains liquidity through disciplined billing 
and collection processes supported by sector payment security 
mechanisms, continuous engagement with counterparties, and 
strong internal controls. This helps protect cash flow, reduce 
short-term borrowing dependence, and improve the predictability 
of capital deployment.
NTPC maintains a disciplined approach to capital management 
to support long-term investments and operational efficiency 
requirements. Funding strategies are aligned with asset lifecycles, 
with a focus on maintaining a balanced capital structure, 
diversified borrowing sources and adequate liquidity. Active 
treasury management helps monitor refinancing, interest-rate 
and liquidity risks while preserving financial flexibility and funding 
readiness for future growth opportunities.
Disciplined working capital management supports NTPC is able 
to sustain its capital investment programme efficiently while 
maintaining financial flexibility. By aligning cash flows with project 
requirements and operational priorities, NTPC i

s able to sustain 
investment momentum across generation, renewable energy and 
infrastructure projects without compromising financial stability.

balanced approach to growth and transition. Alongside investments

business resilience.
NTPC's capital deployment is focused on strengthening India's 
energy security while advancing the development of a cleaner 
and more diversified energy portfolio. At NTPC, we continuously 
invest in high-efficiency thermal capacity and environmental 
technological upgrades to ensure reliability, while scaling our 
renewable energy, pumped storage, and green hydrogen portfolios.

prioritizing execution of readiness, lifecycle returns, and long-term

Ash, a by-product of coal-fired thermal power plants, has now 
gained recognition as a valuable resource material worldwide, 
suitable for diverse applications in the field of Civil Engineering. 
Extensive endeavors are being undertaken at various levels to 
effectively utilize ash in different applications, leading to significant 
achievements in ash utilization.
The latest Gazette Notification of the Ministry of Environment, 
Forests & Climate Change (MoEF&CC), Government of

India, 
introduces guidelines for thermal power plants (TPPs) and ash 
user agencies regarding the utilization of both generated ash and 
legacy ash. In line with the notification, NTPC places significant 
emphasis on sustainable ash utilization as a key focus area within 
its operations. The Company is committed to maximizing the 
utilization of ash across all its power plants. 
During the Financial Year 2025-26, approximately ~100 million 
tons of ash was generated by NTPC Group stations and 107% 
i.e., ~107 million tons of ash had been gainfully utilized in various 
areas such as issue to industries for cement, concrete, bricks/ 
blocks making, road embankment construction, mine filling, land 
development works etc. Twenty stations have achieved 100% ash 
utilization.

Reducing air emissions remains one of NTPC's key environmental priorities. The Company employs a combination of advanced pollution 
control technologies, real-time monitoring systems, and large-scale environmental infrastructure investments to manage emissions 
from thermal operations.
Our investments span Flue Gas Desulphurization (FGD) systems for SOx control, combustion modifications and Low NOx burners for 
NOx reduction, and upgraded Electrostatic Precipitators (ESPs) for Particulate Matter (PM) control. 
Electrostatic Precipitators (ESP): To control particulate matter emissions, NTPC has deployed highly efficient Electrostatic 
Precipitators (ESPs) across its thermal fleet, achieving removal efficiencies of over 99.8%. Renovation & Modernization (R&M) 
of ESPs has been undertaken wherever required. 
Flue Gas Desulphurization (FGD): 55 units of Flue Gas Desulphurization (FGD) systems are commissioned with a total capacity 
of 30,250 megawatts and 90 units of FGD installation is in progress across NTPC plants.
NOx Reduction: NTPC has implemented combustion modifications and De-NOx measures across its thermal fleet to meet 
regulatory emission requirements. Modifications have bee

n completed in all 50 identified units, enabling reduction of nitrogen 
oxide (NOx) emissions to prescribed limits.
CEMS and CAAQMS: Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems (CEMS) and Continuous  Ambient Air Quality Monitoring 
Systems are operational across the fleet, enabling continuous monitoring and regulatory reporting. The real-time monitoring 
data is transmitted to relevant regulatory authorities.
Other Air Emissions Management: NTPC continues to monitor ozone-depleting substances (ODS) and other priority pollutants 
as part of its environmental management framework. Mercury emissions are maintained below the minimum detectable 
limit (MDL), and the Company has completely phased out the use of Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs) across its operations, 
reinforcing its commitment to responsible environmental stewardship.

We track Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions 
on a Group basis, with specific CO₂ emission intensity (tCO₂ per

non-fossil capacity increased by 51.95% in FY 2025-26, and the

At NTPC, we are committed to supporting India's Panchamrit goals 
achieving net zero emissions by 2070, reaching 500 GW of non-fossil 
capacity by 2030, and reducing emissions intensity of GDP by 45% 
by 2030. The Company is pursuing a diversified energy transition 
strategy encompassing renewable energy, green hydrogen, energy 
storage, carbon capture and utilisation, biomass co-firing, nuclear 
energy, and nature-based carbon sinks.
In collaboration with NITI Aayog, we are co-developing a 
comprehensive Net Zero GHG Emissions Roadmap, aligning with 
India's Panchamrit targets while balancing energy security and 
affordability. Separately, NTPC has entered a strategic partnership 
with Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) to formulate an energy 
transition roadmap. NTPC is among the first global energy companies 
to declare an Energy Compact at the UN High-Level Dialogue on 
Energy, committing to measurable SDG7-aligned outcomes.

carbon management strategy through a centralised approach 
to carbon portfolio development, project registration, carbon

opportunities across NTPC and its subsidiaries while supporting the

activities span project registration, verification and issuance, carbon 
trading, capacity building, policy engagement, and participation in 
emerging domestic and international carbon markets.

human rights and labour practices alongside occupational 
health and safety across all employees and contract workforce.

operational excellence required today but also develops the future-
ready capabilities essential for India's energy transition toward a

egulatory expectations, including

(NTPC Green Energy Limited)
Material Listed Subsidiary
NGEL incorporated in April 2022, is a subsidiary of your Company and serves as its flagship 
green energy platform, spearheading the Company’s energy transition initiatives. 
The Company is engaged in the development and implementation of utility-scale solar, wind 
and hybrid power projects, including Ultra Mega Renewable Energy Power Parks (UMREPPs), 
across the country and is also pursuing opportunities in green hydrogen and allied emerging

region of India and operates a diversified portfolio comprising six hydro power stations, three 
gas-based power stations and one solar power station, with an aggregate installed capacity

6 MW under construction.

upon acquisition of 74.496% equity stake from the Government of India. The balance 25.504% 
equity stake is held by the Government of Uttar Pradesh.
THDC has a diversified portfolio comprising hydro, thermal, wind and solar power projects 
with an aggregate capacity of 5,551 MW, including 3,657 MW under operation and 1,644 MW 
under construction. In addition, projects aggregating approximately 10,600 MW are under 
various stages of feasibility studies.
During FY 2025-26, THDC recorded cumulative generation of 13,125.70 MUs.
The Tehri Hydro Power Project and Koteshwar Hydro Electric Project achieved a cumulative 
Plant Availability Factor (PAF) of 80.90%, while the Wind Power Plants and Kasargod Solar 
Power Project recorded Capacity Utilisation Factors (CUF) of 19.35% and 20.76%, respectively.

THDC has paid a dividend of ₹329.25 crore during FY 2025-26 to your Company.

Fuel Mix & Generation
Total electricity generation stood at approximately 1,840 BU in 
FY 2025–26, registering a modest growth of around 1% over FY 
2024–25. Thermal generation declined by about 4%, reflecting the 
increasing penetration of renewable energy, which displaced coal-
based generation, particularly during solar-rich periods.
Renewable electricity generation (including hydro) recorded a 
robust growth of approximately 18%, led by solar (~20% year-on-
year) and wind (~27% year-on-year). Supported by record renewable 
capacity additions and a favourable monsoon that moderated 
cooling demand, coal-based generation declined by around 3.7%, 
marking one of the first notable declines in recent years. Gas-based 
generation also declined significantly by around 18%, while nuclear 
generation witnessed a marginal reduction of approximately 3% 
during the period.
Energy Storage & Grid
Energy storage deployment continued to gain momentum. As per 
the National Generation Adequacy Plan 2026 projections by the 
CEA, India is expected to add ~174 GW / 888 GWh of energy storage 
capacity by 2035, reflecting the growing importance of storage, not 
only for grid balancing but also for integration of rapidly increasing 
variable RE capacity and meet the non-solar hours’ demand.
The national transmission network expanded to approximately 
5 lakh circuit-kilometres, with inter-regional transfer capacity 
increasing to about 120 GW, enhancing grid resilience and 
facilitating renewable integration.
The National Generation Adequacy Plan 2026 has p

rojected India’s 
peak demand to reach ~459 GW and electricity demand to ~3365 
BU by FY 2035–36, underscoring the continued requirement 
for substantial capacity additions across generation and grid 
infrastructure.
Distribution
The Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) continued to 
deliver measurable improvements in the financial and operational 
performance of distribution utilities. The ACS-ARR gap reduced 
significantly from ₹0.78/kWh in FY 2013-14 to ₹0.06/kWh in FY 
2024-25, while AT&C losses reduced from 22.62% in FY 2013-14 
to 15.04% in FY 2024-25, indicating enhanced efficiency and loss 
reduction.
Legacy dues of DISCOMs also witnessed a substantial reduction, 
declining from from ₹1,39,947 crore in 2022 to just ₹3,330 crore 
by March 2026, supported by the implementation of the amended 
Late Payment Surcharge (LPS) Rules.
Under RDSS, smart metering has gained strong traction, with over 
19.79 crore smart meters and 52.53 lakh distribution transformer 
(DT) meters sanctioned, aimed at improving billing efficiency, 
transparency, and demand-side management. 
Key Policy & Regulatory Developments in FY 2025–26
During the year, several regulatory and policy developments were 
introduced to support energy transition, enhance grid flexibility, and 
strengthen market mechanisms:
•	
SHANTI Act, 2025: Landmark legislation replacing the Atomic 
Energy Act 1962 & Civil Liabilities for Nuclear Damage Act, 
2010; permits private Indian companies, foreign companies (up 
to 49% FDI) and joint ventures to build, own and operate nuclear 
plants; paves the way for India’s 100 GW nuclear target by 2047.
•	
Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero: Sectoral 
Insights: Power by NITI Aayog (Feb 2026): The report 
identifies rapid electrification and large-scale clean energy 
deployment as central to achieving the twin goals of India being 
a USD 30 Trillion economy by 2047 and Net Zero economy 
by 2070; projects electricity to account for nearly 60% of the 
total ene

rgy consumption by 2070, with non-fossil sources 
contributing about 98% of power generation; estimates 
cumulative investment requirements of approximately USD 
14.2 trillion in the power sector through 2070 and highlights 
affordable, reliable and low-carbon electricity as a key enabler 
of India’s long-term economic growth and decarbonisation 
pathway.
•	
CERC Tariff Regulations (Second Amendment), 2026: 
Introduced a comprehensive framework for Energy Storage 
Systems (ESS) co-located with thermal plants and ISTS. The 
regulations enable storage for supply to beneficiaries, support 
ancillary services, and enhance renewable energy integration. 
Key provisions include defined norms for battery life (15 years), 
RoE (14%), availability (90%), and efficiency (≥85%). Additional 
provisions include monthly recovery of ash transportation 
costs, incentives for captive coal mining efficiency, and 
introduction of a Regulatory Sandbox to promote innovation. 
•	
Thermal Unit Shutdown Framework (CERC Order, October 
2025): Allows thermal generating units to undertake unit 
shutdown (USD) when scheduled below 50% of capacity, 
improving operational efficiency. Restrictions on peak vs off-
peak declaration ensure grid reliability. 
•	
Deviation Settlement Mechanism (DSM) Amendment, 2025: 
Provides clarity on infirm power injection and scheduling, 
including pricing caps and operational conditions, thereby 
strengthening grid discipline. 
•	
Virtual Power Purchase Agreements (VPPA) Guidelines, 
2025: Establishes a framework enabling consumers to 
meet RPO/RCO obligations through RECs, while facilitating 
renewable procurement without physical power transfer. 
•	
Renewable Generation Obligation (RGO) Clarification: The 
Ministry of Power has made RGO compliance voluntary for 
thermal stations commissioned after April 2025, providing 
greater flexibility in renewable capacity planning. 
•	
Renewable Consumption Obligation (RCO): Mandates 
increasing renewable consumption targe

ts from ~30% in FY 
2024–25 to ~43% by FY 2029–30 for DISCOMs, open access 
consumers, and captive users. Compliance mechanisms 
include direct consumption, RECs, and buyout provisions. 
•	
Electricity Rules Amendment – Captive Generation (2026): 
Expands the definition of ownership (including subsidiaries 
and holding structures), facilitating greater participation in 
captive power projects. 
•	
Draft Policy Developments: Draft amendments to the 
Electricity Act, 2003 and the National Electricity Policy, 2026 
have been issued for stakeholder consultation, indicating 
continued policy evolution in the sector.
•	
RE Manufacturing Boost: GST on renewable equipment 
reduced from 12% to 5%; launch of Renewable Energy 
Equipment Import Monitoring System (REEIMS); incentives 
for domestic battery manufacturing.
•	
Customs Duty Exemption: Union Budget 2026–27 extended 
customs duty exemption on imports for all nuclear power 
projects until 2035.
•	
Electricity (Amendment) Rules 2025: Allowed integration 
of consumer-owned energy storage systems with the grid, 
boosting distributed flexibility.

NTPC’s Strategic Positioning in Global Context
As India advances towards its vision of becoming a Viksit Bharat 
by 2047, its electricity demand is projected to grow at 6–6.5% per

while reinforcing its pivotal role in supporting India’s growth 
aspirations.

Fuel Security
NTPC has adopted a robust and forward-looking strategy to ensure

fuel security for its extensive fleet of thermal power plants. This 
strategy focuses on mitigating risks associated with fuel shortages, 
price fluctuations, and logistical challenges by enhancing domestic 
coal production, diversifying procurement sources, and eliminating 
imports. 
The company has secured 100% fuel tie-up for its thermal capacity 
through long-term Fuel Supply Agreements (FSAs) with coal 
companies (CIL & SCCL), with a total Annual Contracted Quantity 
(ACQ) of 256.92 MMT across the NTPC group. During FY 2025–26, 
ACQ materialization from coal companies stood at 84%. NTPC 
further strengthened its fuel security by sourcing 43.5 MMT of coal 
from its captive mines. 
NTPC has also procured domestic coal on FOR (Free on Rail) 
destination basis from commercial mines & surplus coal from 
captive blocks through competitive bidding. Thus, NTPC offset 
the shortfall from linked sources without procuring imported coal, 
thereby reducing the overall cost of power generation.
Captive Coal Mining
To strengthen fuel security, NTPC continues to expand its captive 
coal mining portfolio, with a target to increase production capacity 
from 91.6 MMTPA to 100 MMTPA and beyond.
To enhance operational focus, NTPC has consolidated its mining 
activities under its wholly owned subsidiary, NTPC Mining Limited 
(NML). With the transfer of Pakri Barwadih Coal mine on 01st April 
2026, all the six coal mines have been transferred from NTPC 
to NML. While one mine – Badam- is under development, NML 
currently operates five mines - Pakri-Barwadih, Dulanga, Talaipalli, 
Chatti-Bariatu, and Kerandari, all of which have been declared 
commercial.
Coal production from the captive mines, including production from 
the Amelia mine operated by THDC India Limited, stood at 48.65 
MMT during the year, 6.22% higher than the previous fiscal.
Operations from Badam mine are expected to commence in 
FY 2026–27, while progress continues on the Banhardih mine 
(PVUNL). NML has also secure

d its first commercial coal block, 
North-Dadhu (Eastern Part) with the mining plan approved, and 
development activities in progress.
In addition to coal, NML is actively pursuing diversification into 
critical minerals, supported by strategic collaborations with leading 
institutions and industry partners.
Through these initiatives, NTPC aims to build a resilient, cost-
effective domestic fuel supply base, while supporting long-term 
energy security and emerging transition requirements.
Power Trading (NVVN)
During FY 2025-26, NTPC strengthened its diversified energy and 
sustainability portfolio through its subsidiary NVVN, delivering 
robust growth across power trading, renewable energy, waste-
to-energy and carbon management businesses. Power trading 
volume increased by 13% to 46.38 BU, driven by strong growth 
in exchange-based and cross-border power trading, including 
addition of the Punatsangchu-II hydro project in Bhutan. The 
Company also expanded its renewable energy portfolio with over 
227 MW of rooftop and ground-mounted solar projects under 
commissioning, construction and tendering stages. Significant 
progress was achieved in waste-to-energy projects at Varanasi, 
Noida, Gorakhpur, Bhopal and Hubballi-Dharwad, while battery 
energy storage projects and consultancy assignments further 
strengthened the clean energy portfolio. During the year, NVVN also 
enhanced its participation in emerging carbon markets, expanded 
gas trading operations, and implemented multiple digital initiatives 
for power exchange bidding, analytics and cross-border scheduling, 
reinforcing its focus on innovation, sustainability and integrated 
energy solutions.
Renewable Energy (NTPC Group)
NTPC continues to expand its capacity in line with India’s growth 
trajectory while advancing its commitment to energy transition and 
net-zero objectives. The Company has set an ambitious target of 
244 GW (and 6 GW PSP) installed capacity by 2037, including RE 
capacity targets of 60 G

W by 2032 and 136 GW by 2037.
During FY 2025–26, NTPC achieved a key milestone by crossing

FUTURE OUTLOOK
SWOT Analysis — NTPC Group
The following matrix presents a structured assessment of NTPC’s internal capabilities and the external environment shaping its strategic 
choices:
Strengths
NTPC continues to maintain its leadership position as India’s 
largest integrated power utility, with a group installed capacity 
exceeding 89 GW. During FY26, the Company achieved a record 
capacity addition of 9,618 MW, reflecting strong project execution 
capabilities. Operational performance remains robust, with coal-
based stations operating at a Plant Load Factor (PLF) of ~72%, 
higher than the national average of ~65.5%.
The Company has developed a diversified portfolio spanning 
thermal, hydro, renewable energy, nuclear, and emerging areas 
such as green hydrogen, enabling it to effectively participate in the 
evolving energy landscape. Even as NTPC continues to undertake 
one of the sector’s largest capital expenditure programmes, it 
improved its debt-equity ratio from 1.15x in FY25 to 1.09x in FY26, 
reflecting prudent leverage management, stronger balance sheet 
resilience, and greater headroom to access low-cost debt for the 
upcoming growth cycle.
The steady growth in PAT and net worth further underscores 
the Company’s strong financial discipline along with sustained 
operating cash flows, and improved debt service coverage and 
interest coverage ratios. Commercial performance remains strong 
with 100% billing realisation and secured payment mechanisms 
under tri

partite agreements. Additionally, the Company has 
demonstrated sustained improvement in ESG performance and 
sustainability initiatives, as evidenced by significant upgrades in its 
ratings from several reputed agencies.
Weaknesses
The increasing penetration of renewable energy has led to a 
decline in coal PLF (down by ~5 percentage points), impacting 
utilisation levels of thermal assets. Gas-based capacity continues 
to remain underutilised, primarily due to fuel availability and pricing 
constraints.
Opportunities
India’s electricity demand is expected to grow at 6–6.5% per 
annum, driven by increased electrification, digitalisation, electric 
mobility, and data centre expansion, providing significant growth 
opportunities. The Government’s target of achieving 500 GW of 
non-fossil capacity by 2030 necessitates accelerated renewable 
capacity addition, positioning NTPC to expand its clean energy 
portfolio.
Policy support for nuclear expansion for reaching capacity of 100 
GW by 2047, including enabling provisions for private participation, 
offers long-term diversification opportunities. The Company is also 
well placed to leverage emerging areas such as green hydrogen, 
green ammonia, and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), including 
export-oriented initiatives.
Additionally, opportunities exist in carbon markets, with NTPC 
having already generated carbon credits, and in the commercial 
and industrial (C&I) segment through virtual power purchase 
agreements (VPPAs) and open access mechanisms.
Threats 
The increasing share of renewable energy (RE) introduces 
operational challenges, including the “duck curve” effect, 
characterised by periods of surplus solar generation and steep 
ramping requirements for thermal capacities. Higher penetration 
of variable RE increases grid integration complexity, requiring 
enhanced flexibility, storage solutions, and system balancing 
capabilities. While this provides an opportunity for the NTPC’s 
capacities to operate as pe

aking capacities, the rate of increase in 
peak demand may surpass the rate of growth of energy demand 
leading to sharper peaks owing to cooling load, data centre demand 
and EV demand expansion, which maybe difficult for coal plants 
to serve effectively. Further, a downward trend in the BESS tariffs 
is also making solar + BESS more attractive to meet the non-solar 
hours peaking requirement, competing with new thermal capacities. 
However, a level of mitigation of the risk due to flexible operation 
of coal-based capacities is provided by CERC’s tariff regulations 
offering higher percentage of ROE for higher ramp rate capability. 
With higher projections of thermal capacities under National 
Generation Adequacy Plan 2026, up to 315 GW by 2035-36, CEA 
has given strong indications of the continued importance of coal-
based capacities in maintaining reliability of the grid whether by 
way of base-load generation, ramping capability or reserve peaking 
provisions.
For the high-growth plans of RE capacity addition by NTPC Group, 
the threat is in form of excess solar supply during day-time 
compressing market prices and causing high price volatility through 
the day, thus eroding the margins in an already competitive play 
space. Transmission bottlenecks are exacerbating the curtailment 
of RE supply from new and upcoming projects leading to revenue 
loss.
CAPACITY TARGETS
The Company revised its total capacity target upward to 149 GW by 
2032 and 244 GW by 2037, from the earlier 130 GW by 2032. This 
reflects the government’s accelerated 500 GW non-fossil target 
and India’s rising power demand trajectory. By 2032, the fuel mix 
will comprise 60 GW of renewables, ~84 GW of thermal (all future 
additions via ultra-supercritical technology), and a growing nuclear 
portfolio.

Revenue From Operations 
Revenue from operations primarily comprises of variable charges 
for electricity generation and fixed (capacity) charges towards 
recovery of fixed costs. Together, these two components constitute 
more than 95% of revenue from operations in both the financial 
years & the same have been accounted for in line with the CERC 
tariff regulations 2024 as amended from time to time.
Revenue from operations decreased by 2.67 % from ₹1,70,037.37 
crore in FY 2024-25 to ₹1,65,493.74 crore in FY 2025-26, mainly 
due to Lower Energy Sent Out (ESO) by 19.844 BU from 347.292 
BU in FY 2024 25 to 327.448 BU in FY 2025-26(due to lower power 
demand). This is partly offset by commissioning of new capacities 
during the years, favourable tariff orders & 2nd amendment to 
CERC tariff regulations. (Refer note 38 at page 263)
PLF of Coal stations in FY 2025-26 was 72.04% against rest of India 
coal PLF of 63.20% underscoring the Company’s strong operational 
performance and maintenance capabilities.
Other Income 
Other Income has reduced by 3.32% from ₹4,376.12 Crore in FY 
2024-25 to ₹4,230.86 Crore in FY 2025-26 mainly due to higher 
scrap sale and Provision written back in previous year partly 
offset by Interest on income tax refund received in Current year. 
(Refer note 39 at page 264)
Total Expenses 
Total expenses are largely driven by fuel cost (including electricity 
purchased for trading), which constituted about 63% of total 
expenses followed by other expenses 15%, depreciation 11%, 
finance cost 7% and

employee cost 4%.

Fuel Cost
Fuel cost is incurred on consumption of Coal, Gas, Oil & Biomass 
used for electricity generation. Fuel cost has reduced by 8.71% from 
₹97,060.24 Crore in FY 2024-25 to ₹88,605.04 Crore in FY 2025-26 
due to lower commercial generation of 20.271 BU in FY 2025-26 & 
decrease in average price of domestic coal by 1.48% from ₹3,522/
MT in FY 2024-25 to ₹3,470/MT in FY 2025-26. (Refer note 40 at 
page 266)
Employee Benefit Expense 
Employee benefit expense has increased marginally by 2.07 % from 
₹5,724.67 crore in FY 2024-25 to ₹5,843.12 crore in FY 2025-26. 
(Refer note 41 at page 266)
Finance Cost 
Finance cost has reduced by 5.56% from ₹11,057.04 Crore in 
FY 2024-25 to ₹10,442.18 Crore in FY 2025-26, mainly due to 
repayment of loans and a reduction in rate of borrowings resulting 
from proactive restructuring and refinancing of loans. The weighted 
average rate of borrowings has decreased from 6.61% in FY 2024-
25 to 5.98% in FY 2025-26. (Refer note 42 at page 266)
Depreciation 
Depreciation expense increased by 6.48% from ₹15055.84 
Crore in FY 2024-25 to ₹16,030.85 Crore in FY 2025-26, due to 
commissioning of additional capacity and capital expenditure on 
existing stations. (Refer note 43 at page 267)
Other Expenses 
Other expenses mainly comprise of repair & maintenance 
expense, Exchange rate variation (ERV), Station overheads & Ash 
transportation expenses. Other expenses increased by 23.93% 
from ₹18,111.60 Crore to ₹22,445.63 Crore, mainly on account 
of unfavourable exchange rate variation, for which regulatory 
income has been created to the extent allowable under CERC tariff 
regulations and provision for impairment of investment of group 
companies. (Refer note 44 at page 268)
EBITDA 
EBITDA (Including regulatory adjustments) increased by 4.84%

from ₹49,785.05 crore in FY 2024-25 to Rs 52,195.07 Crore 
in FY 2025-26, primarily on account of higher revenue from 
commissioning of new capacities during the years, favourable 
tariff orders & the 2nd amendment to CERC tariff regulations partly 
offset by higher provisions for impairment on investment in group 
companies and tariff adjustment etc.
Profit after tax (PAT) 
Profit after tax increased by 17.88% from ₹19,649.41 Crore in FY 
2024-25 to ₹23,162.22 Crore for FY 2025-26. The improvement 
was primarily driven by higher regulated equity on account of 
commissioning of additional capacity and capital expenditure in 
existing stations, higher dividend income from group companies, 
favourable tariff orders & impact of 2nd amendment to CERC tariff 
regulations.
Return on Net Worth (RONW) 
Return on net worth increased from 12.61% in FY 2024 25 to 13.77% 
in FY 2025 26, reflecting higher profitability, partly moderated by an 
increase in net worth on account of retained earnings.

increase in current liabilities vis-à-vis current assets. However, the ratio continues to remain below unity, indicating reliance on efficient 
working capital management, strong operating cash flows, and access to short-term funding lines to meet near-term obligations.
The debt–equity ratio declined, indicating strengthening of the capital structure through higher internal accruals. Operating and net profit 
margins improved during the year, driven by Capacity additions, favourable tariff orders & 2nd amendment to CERC tariff regulations,

separate report on the adequacy and operating effectiveness of 
internal financial controls over financial reporting, which forms

reviews the financial statements and audit 
observations in consultation with the Internal and Statutory Auditors

Corporate Governance refers to adoption of sound management 
practices, compliance with applicable laws, and adherence 
to ethical standards to achieve the Company’s objectives, 
enhancing stakeholder value, and fulfilling social responsibilities. It 
encompasses the relationships among various stakeholders, such 
as shareholders, management, employees, customers, suppliers 
and the community at large. The objective of corporate governance 
is to manage the business to maximise long-term value, while 
ensuring the protection of stakeholders’ interests.
This report is prepared in accordance with the provisions of SEBI 
(Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 
(‘Listing Regulations’) and the Guidelines on Corporate Governance 
for Central Public Sector Enterprises, 2010 (‘CG Guidelines’) 
issued by the Department of Public Enterprises (‘DPE’), Ministry of 
Finance, Government of India, highlighted corporate governance 
methodology at NTPC Limited (‘NTPC’/ ‘the Company’).
1.	 NTPC’s Corporate Governance Philosophy
OUR CORPORATE GOVERNANCE PHILOSOPHY
“As a good corporate governance citizen, our company 
is committed to sound corporate practices based on 
conscience, openness, fairness, professionalism and 
accountability besides building confidence in its various 
stakeholders, thereby paving the way for the long term 
success.”
	
The Company’s philosophy on corporate governance oversees 
business 
strategies 
and 
ensures 
fiscal 
accountability, 
ethical corporate behaviour and fairness to all stakeholders 
comprising investors, Employees, cus

tomers, regulators, 
suppliers and the society at large. Our dedicated initiatives in 
fostering and maintaining the highest standards of governance 
are presented in this report.
2.	 Board of Directors
	
The Board of Directors, as the apex body constituted by 
shareholders, provides strategic direction and leadership to 
the Company and oversees management policies and their 
effectiveness, with a focus on long-term shareholder and 
stakeholder interests. It is responsible for driving economy, 
efficiency, and effectiveness in operations, while ensuring 
value creation and sustainable growth. The Board discharges 
its functions in accordance with the Companies Act, 2013 
(‘the Act’), Listing Regulations, the Company’s Memorandum 
and Articles of Association, Maharatna Guidelines & CG 
Guidelines issued by DPE, and other applicable directions of 
the Government of India.
2.1	 Composition of Board
	
NTPC is a Government Company under Section 2(45) of the 
Act and, according to its Articles of Association, all Directors 
are appointed by the President of India. The approved Board 
composition included six (6) Functional Directors (including 
the Chairman & Managing Director), two (2) Government 
Nominee Directors, and eight (8) Independent Directors—one 
(1) of whom is required to be a woman in accordance with 
Listing Regulations. However, as on 31st March 2026, the Board 
comprised six (6) Functional Directors, two (2) Government 
Nominee Directors, and only five (5) Independent Directors 
including one (1) woman Independent Director. During FY 
2025–26, numbers of Independent Directors were less 
than half of the Board. Further, the mandates regarding the 
presence of a woman independent director and at least 50% 
non-executive directors were not fulfilled until 18th May 2025. 
NTPC has requested the Administrative Ministry i.e. Ministry 
of Power (‘MoP’) for appointments of the necessary number of 
independent and non-executive directors.
	
The present strength of

the Board reflects judicious mix of 
professionalism, competence and sound knowledge which 
enables the Board to provide effective leadership to the 
Company.
2.1.1 Key skills, expertise, competencies of the Board of Directors
	
The Board comprises qualified members possessing the 
necessary skills, competence and expertise to effectively 
contribute to Board and Committee deliberations. The Board 
of Directors had approved the job description, qualifications 
and experience requirements for Board-level positions. The 
candidates for the position of Functional Director on the Board 
of the Company are selected by the Public Enterprise Selection 
Board. 
	
The Board of Directors had also decided that Independent 
Directors nominated by the Government of India are expected 
to possess expertise in diverse fields such as Technical/
Engineering, Economics, Human Resource Management, 
Regulatory Framework, Management, Research & Development, 
Academics, Energy & Power Sector and Finance & Banking.
